title: Remember When We Just Remembered Things?
author: Rich Carr
summary: Rich Carr opens with a dinner where four friends agreed to keep phones in their pockets and then spent twenty minutes failing to recall who played the sheriff in Jaws, until the name Roy Scheider arrived at 2 a.m. He uses the story to argue that the struggle to retrieve an answer is what makes it stick, whereas a search engine hands over the answer before anyone wanted it and it slides off. Curiosity, he says, activates the brain's reward system and prepares memory to hold on, and it is the starting point of what he calls Premium Thinking. He distinguishes covering information, which hands people answers early, from uncovering it, which lets them reach. The piece ends with applications for individuals, teams, and writers: let a question sit, present the problem before the explanation, and leave the audience one step to take on their own.
points: Reaching for an answer, including through wrong guesses, builds the neural paths that make the eventual answer memorable.
Instant answers from search or AI deliver information before curiosity has opened memory to receive it, producing what the author calls instant amnesia.
Covering material hands people answers early, while uncovering it lets them reach, which is why sixty-slide decks are forgotten and real problems are remembered.
Teachers and leaders can leave the gap between what people know and want to know open long enough for it to do its work.
For teams, presenting the problem first and letting people argue and guess wrong gives the eventual answer somewhere to land.
quotes: When you badly want an answer, your brain gets ready to keep it. Curiosity switches on the same reward system that lights up when you’re hungry and smell dinner, and that system tells your memory to pay attention and hold on.
A search engine drops the answer into a closed hand, before anyone wanted it, and it slides right off.
It was the twenty minutes of reaching for the answer that did the real work. Every face we described and every wrong name we tried and tossed laid down another path toward the right one.
That itch of almost knowing is uncomfortable, and it’s also the moment a brain stops receiving and starts working.
Covering the information for something hands people the answer before their brain wants it. Uncovering lets them reach for it.
The phone in your pocket is a wonderful tool, and I’m keeping mine. Every time it answers a question in four seconds, though, it takes away the reach, and the reach is where the remembering happens.
Bring them the problem first. Let them argue about it, guess wrong, and get close.
